t: Minimum Addition to Make Integer Beautiful
o: Find the smallest x ≥ 0 so digitSum(n + x) ≤ target, n up to 1e12. Adding x only helps meaningfully when it causes carries that zero out low digits — e.g., 467 → 500. Greedy strategy: while digitSum exceeds target, round the current value up to the next multiple of 10^p (zeroing digit p and below), increasing p each time. This enumerates exactly the candidate values n+x in increasing order that could have small digit sums, so the first success is optimal. Example: 467 → 470 (11) → 480 → 490 → 500 (5 ≤ 6), giving x = 33.
k: Any beautiful n+x must have been reached by zeroing out some suffix of digits via carries.
Rounding up to successive multiples of 10, 100, 1000, … enumerates candidates in increasing x order.
At most ~13 iterations since digit sums shrink geometrically with each rounding.

a.i: Try x = 0, 1, 2, … until digitSum(n+x) ≤ target. Correct but far too slow for n = 1e12 with small target (x can be ~1e12).
s: Loop x upward, compute digit sum of n+x.
Return first x meeting the bound.
a.t: O(x · digits) — exponential in the worst case; not viable for large n

a.i: Candidates worth testing are n rounded up to multiples of 10, then 100, etc., because those are precisely the points where carries collapse digit sums. The sequence of required additions is strictly increasing, so the first candidate with digitSum ≤ target is the answer.
s: While digitSum(n + base) > target: base = (base // p + 1) * p; p *= 10.
a.t: O(digits²) ≈ 13² — each rounding pass recomputes the digit sum

w: The rounding greedy is the intended solution; note it never overshoots because any smaller x would leave more low-order digits intact and hence a larger-or-equal digit sum among tested candidates. Careful with 64-bit types (n up to 1e12 fits in long long; JS numbers are safe below 2^53). Edge case: n already beautiful → 0. Follow-up: minimize x such that digit sum equals exactly target.
